hook: Galileo is said to have timed a swinging cathedral lamp against his pulse and noticed that big swings and small swings took the same time. Three centuries of pendulum clocks were built on that fact. This lesson shows what does set the time of a swing, and the two things that surprisingly do not.

figure.caption: What sets the period of a block on a spring and of a pendulum, and what does not.

chain.cause: A larger mass on the same spring
chain.effect: accelerates less for the same restoring force, so it takes longer to turn around: T grows as √m
gives a larger restoring force at each position, so the period shrinks as 1/√k
means more distance to cover but proportionally more force and speed, so the period does not change

chain.cause: For a pendulum, a heavier bob
chain.effect: has more weight pulling it back and more inertia in exactly the same ratio, so its period does not change either

ideas: The period T is the time for one full cycle; the frequency is f = 1/T, in hertz (cycles per second). Time many cycles and divide to measure T well.
A block on a spring: T = 2π√(m/k). More mass, longer period; stiffer spring, shorter period. No amplitude and no g in it.
A simple pendulum at small angles: T = 2π√(ℓ/g). Longer string, longer period; stronger gravitational field, shorter period. No mass in it.
Functional dependence: four times the mass (or length) doubles the period, because T goes as the square root.

misconception.wrong: A heavier pendulum bob swings more slowly, because T = 2π√(m/k) has the mass in it.
misconception.right: That formula is for a block on a spring. A pendulum's period is T = 2π√(ℓ/g): the heavier bob is pulled back harder but has more inertia in the same ratio, so its period is unchanged.

summary: The period of a block on a spring is T = 2π√(m/k) and that of a small-angle pendulum is T = 2π√(ℓ/g); neither depends on the amplitude, the pendulum's period does not depend on the bob's mass, and f = 1/T.
